messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame was eighteen years old and had been working at the tax consultancy firm for only two months when the assault happened. The event itself is something he can only access in jagged pieces. He had stayed late to finish a client file, alone in the quiet office building. The memory comes back not as a story, but as a series of blindingly clear snapshots: the face of the cleaning crew supervisor, a man he had seen before, his expression shifting from a benign smile to something else entirely as the office door clicked shut behind him. There are images of the beige carpet fibres pressed against his cheek, the blinding fluorescent light overhead, and the man’s shouting, which seemed to fill the entire world. The most visceral part of the memory, the part that ambushes him without warning, is the metallic taste of blood in his mouth.

In the six months since, Kwame’s world has been systematically dismantled by the echoes of that night. The triggers are everywhere, turning his new career into a minefield. A manager shouting a question across the open-plan office is no longer just a sound; it’s a direct threat. The sudden noise sends a jolt of pure adrenaline through him, making him feel exposed and hunted right at his desk. In these moments, his perception of danger sharpens to an unbearable degree, and he is certain that something terrible is about to happen again. This heightened sense of threat means that even ordinary sounds, like the heavy oak door to the conference room slamming shut, become precursors to violence in his mind, causing him to flinch violently in his chair.

These triggers do not just ignite fear; they are a direct line back to the trauma. The sound of a door opening unexpectedly behind him is enough to flood his mind with the image of the supervisor’s face, so clear and detailed it feels like it’s happening right now. With the image comes the phantom taste of blood, so vivid it makes him gag. Conversely, when his general state of anxiety is high, feeling cornered by a deadline or simply unsafe on a crowded subway, the memories seem to surface on their own. The feeling of overwhelming dread can bring back the fragmented images, or sometimes just the raw emotion of terror and helplessness from that night, a feeling so potent it leaves him breathless and disoriented, unsure of where he is.

This creates a devastating, self-perpetuating cycle. A flashback, even a fleeting one, leaves him raw and hyper-aware, priming him to notice every potential danger. After an episode, he finds himself scanning doorways, tracking every male colleague’s movements, his hearing attuned to the slightest sound that might signal a repeat of the shouting. This constant state of threat monitoring makes him exquisitely sensitive to the very triggers that brought the memory back in the first place. The fear itself has become a magnet for the memories; when a stranger stands too close on his commute, the immediate sense of being trapped and vulnerable is enough to conjure the images he spends every waking moment trying to suppress.

The consequences have been profound. Kwame no longer goes to unfamiliar places, which has meant turning down opportunities to visit new client offices, a crucial part of his job. His colleagues have noticed his jumpiness; one patted him on the shoulder to congratulate him on a well-prepared file, and Kwame reacted with such alarm that the man recoiled, apologizing profusely. He now makes excuses to avoid being the last one in the office and refuses to be in a meeting room alone with any man, a behaviour that is isolating him from his team. He came to therapy after his manager gently noted his performance was slipping and asked if everything was alright. Kwame couldn't answer, but he knew he couldn’t continue living in a world where every slammed door was an attack and every man was a potential threat. He is terrified that he is permanently broken, but a small part of him hopes he can one day feel safe in his own skin again.
